Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 31
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Vignette:
Mara, a 31-year-old Oceania woman and professor at a local university, has been struggling with persistent psychological distress following a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that occurred several months ago. The trauma of the event has left deep marks on her psyche, influencing every aspect of her daily life. The accident happened during rush hour as she was driving home from work. Mara had come to believe that any sudden jolt or loud noise could bring back terrifying sensations of being trapped and out of control. She recalled feeling detached from herself and the world around her at the moment of impact, a dissociative experience that continued in flashes throughout her day. Since then, conversations about accidents or seeing images of car crashes on television have triggered intense episodes where Mara would suddenly feel as if she were reliving the accident. Her husband had noticed her becoming superalert and watchful even in their own home, often waking up multiple times during the night to check that everything was safe. Her memories of the event are fragmented; moments of clarity where she vividly remembers the sound of shattering glass and the smell of smoke, but other details remain a complete blank. When trying to recount the event, Mara loses track of her thoughts and struggles to piece together a coherent narrative. The disjointed nature of her memories has left her feeling isolated and adrift. In the months following the accident, Mara found herself increasingly withdrawn from social interactions and professional commitments. She had begun avoiding discussions about traffic incidents and even stopped driving altogether, opting instead for public transportation or walking long distances to work. This decision took a toll on both her professional life and personal relationships. At the university, she found it difficult to engage fully in academic discussions, often feeling detached from her usual enthusiasm. Mara’s husband noted that she seemed distant and unhappy, no longer showing interest in activities they once enjoyed together. She had come to believe that she used to be a happy person but now felt miserable all the time. The sense of belonging at work and within their community was lost; she often felt as though she did not fit in anywhere anymore. Her perception of meaning in life had also diminished, leaving her feeling like everything around her lacked purpose or significance. Despite these challenges, what finally brought Mara to seek help was a particularly distressing episode where she experienced a vivid flashback during one of her lectures. In that moment, she felt as if the classroom was spinning and became overwhelmed with anxiety. She realized then that her life had become unmanageable and she needed support to regain control. Mara is now in therapy, hoping to find ways to reconnect with the world around her and rediscover a sense of meaning and happiness. She acknowledges her fears and hopes that through therapy, she can learn to manage her symptoms and reengage with her daily life without feeling constantly on edge or disconnected from reality.
